chapter_guidelines.content:
The principles of multiple coding of injuries should be followed in coding 
fractures. Fractures of specified sites are coded individually by site in 
accordance with both the provisions within categories S02, S12, S22, S32, S42, 
S49, S52, S59, S62, S72, S79, S82, S89, S92 and the level of detail furnished by 
medical record content. 
 
A fracture not indicated as open or closed should be coded to closed. A fracture 
not indicated whether displaced or not displaced should be coded to displaced. 
 
More specific guidelines are as follows:

sections.content:
fractures 
Traumatic fractures are coded using the appropriate 7th character for 
initial encounter (A, B, C) for each encounter where the patient is 
receiving active treatment for the fracture. The appropriate 7th character 
for initial encounter should also be assigned for a patient who delayed 
seeking treatment for the fracture or nonunion. 
 
Fractures are coded using the appropriate 7th character for subsequent 
care for encounters after the patient has completed active treatment of the 
fracture and is receiving routine care for the fracture during the healing 
or recovery phase. 
 
Care for complications of surgical treatment for fracture repairs during 
the healing or recovery phase should be coded with the appropriate 
complication codes. 
 
Care of complications of fractures, such as malunion and nonunion, 
should be reported with the appropriate 7th character for subsequent care 
with nonunion (K, M, N,) or subsequent care with malunion (P, Q, R). 
 
Malunion/nonunion: The appropriate 7th character for initial encounter 
should also be assigned for a patient who delayed seeking treatment for 
the fracture or nonunion. 
 
The open fracture designations in the assignment of the 7th character for 
fractures of the forearm, femur and lower leg, including ankle are based 
on the Gustilo open fracture classification. When the Gustilo 
classification type is not specified for an open fracture, the 7th character 
for open fracture type I or II should be assigned (B, E, H, M, Q). 
 
A code from category M80, not a traumatic fracture code, should be used 
for any patient with known osteoporosis who suffers a fracture, even if 
the patient had a minor fall or trauma, if that fall or trauma would not 
usually break a normal, healthy bone. 
 
See Section I.C.13. Osteoporosis. 
 
The aftercare Z codes should not be used for aftercare for traumatic 
fractures. For aftercare of a traumatic fracture, assign the acute fracture 
code with the appropriate 7th character.
sections.title: Initial vs. subsequent encounter for fractures

sections.content:
Multiple fractures are sequenced in accordance with the severity of the 
fracture.
sections.title: Multiple fractures sequencing

sections.content:
For physeal fractures, assign only the code identifying the type of 
physeal fracture. Do not assign a separate code to identify the specific 
bone that is fractured.

text:
Encounter Summary:
- 42-year-old male admitted for trauma.
- Rib fracture laterality is inconsistent across the record.
- Admission and initial documentation state left-sided injury, while CT, operative record, and discharge diagnosis state right-sided injury.
- Operative documentation states fixation of the right 5th rib fracture.

Documentation Gaps:
1. Laterality conflict for the rib fracture
- Why it matters: Rib fracture coding requires side specificity. Category S22.3 distinguishes right side vs left side, so conflicting laterality prevents reliable diagnosis code assignment.
- Evidence quotes:
  - “Admission diagnosis: left rib fracture.”
  - “Discharge diagnosis: right rib fracture.”
  - “Initial diagnosis: left chest trauma.”
  - “CT report: right rib fracture.”
  - “Operative record: right chest 5th rib fracture fixation.”
- Minimal clarification needed: Confirm the correct laterality of the rib fracture and whether any left-sided chest injury/rib fracture was actually present.

2. Specific fracture description not aligned across documentation
- Why it matters: Traumatic fractures should be coded to the highest level of detail supported by the record. The excerpt supports a single rib level in the operative note (“5th rib”), but the principal diagnosis documentation is inconsistent and does not clearly reconcile site/laterality across the encounter.
- Evidence quotes:
  - “Admission diagnosis: left rib fracture.”
  - “Discharge diagnosis: right rib fracture.”
  - “Operative record: right chest 5th rib fracture fixation.”
  - “CT report: right rib fracture.”
- Minimal clarification needed: Confirm whether the treated injury was a single right 5th rib fracture and whether that should be the final diagnosis description.

Proposed Provider Queries:
1. Topic: Rib fracture laterality clarification
- Reason query is needed: The chart contains conflicting laterality for the traumatic rib fracture, preventing consistent final diagnosis documentation and code assignment.
- Evidence quote:
  - “Admission diagnosis: left rib fracture.”
  - “Discharge diagnosis: right rib fracture.”
  - “Operative record: right chest 5th rib fracture fixation.”
  - “CT report: right rib fracture.”
  - “Initial diagnosis: left chest trauma.”
- Non-leading query text:
  - “The record contains conflicting documentation regarding the side of the rib injury. Admission documents note ‘left rib fracture’ and ‘left chest trauma,’ while the CT report, operative record, and discharge diagnosis document a right rib fracture, including ‘right chest 5th rib fracture fixation.’ For this encounter, please clarify the final diagnosis for the rib fracture laterality and site.”
- Suggested response options:
  - Right rib fracture
  - Left rib fracture
  - Bilateral rib injuries/fractures
  - Chest trauma without rib fracture
  - Other, please specify
  - Clinically undetermined

2. Topic: Final fracture specificity clarification
- Reason query is needed: The operative note identifies “right chest 5th rib fracture fixation,” but the diagnosis list does not consistently reflect the same specificity.
- Evidence quote:
  - “Operative record: right chest 5th rib fracture fixation.”
  - “CT report: right rib fracture.”
- Non-leading query text:
  - “Based on the available documentation, please clarify the final fracture description that should be reported for this encounter.”
- Suggested response options:
  - Single right 5th rib fracture
  - Single right rib fracture, rib number not clinically specified
  - Left rib fracture
  - Multiple rib fractures
  - Other, please specify
  - Clinically undetermined

Coding Specificity Checklist:
- Confirm fracture laterality: right vs left vs bilateral.
- Confirm whether this was a single rib fracture or multiple rib fractures.
- If single, document the rib involved if clinically known (operative note states 5th rib).
- Ensure discharge diagnosis reconciles with imaging and operative documentation.
- For traumatic fracture coding, assign to the highest level of specificity supported by the final reconciled record.
- Relevant coding family in excerpt: S22.3 = fracture of one rib, with laterality-specific subcategories including right side and left side.

Risk Flags:
- Direct contradiction in laterality:
  - “Admission diagnosis: left rib fracture” vs “Discharge diagnosis: right rib fracture.”
- Potential copied-forward or intake-history error:
  - “Initial diagnosis: left chest trauma” conflicts with later imaging/procedure documentation on the right.
- Procedure/diagnosis mismatch risk:
  - Operative treatment is for the right 5th rib, so unresolved left-vs-right conflict could lead to inaccurate diagnosis reporting.
- Insufficient evidence to query open/closed, displaced/nondisplaced, or encounter phase beyond active treatment details shown in the excerpt.

Specialist Trace:
- Medical Coding Expert: Consulted.
  - Requested: coding specificity issues and compliant query opportunities for the provided excerpt.
  - Accepted: the coding relevance that rib fracture coding is laterality-specific under S22.3 and that traumatic fractures should be coded to the highest level of detail supported by documentation.
  - Rejected/unused: any unsupported code assignment or procedure-code selection, because the excerpt does not provide enough complete operative detail for definitive code assignment from this note alone.
- AMBOSS Expert: Not consulted.
  - Rationale: no clinical diagnostic criteria clarification was needed; the core issue is documentation inconsistency.
- CDI/Web Search Expert: Not consulted.
  - Rationale: current external guidance was not necessary to identify this chart-based documentation conflict.

Bottom line:
- The primary CDI issue is a laterality conflict. A compliant provider query should reconcile whether the final diagnosis is a right rib fracture, left rib fracture, bilateral injury, or another clarified condition, using the exact conflicting chart statements above.
